steps.body: Estimating a fraction product compares each group to one whole. If 5/6 is nearly a whole, then 7 × 5/6 is a little under 7.
steps.narration: Estimating a fraction product compares each group to one whole. If 5/6 is nearly a whole, then 7 × 5/6 is a little under 7.

widget.prompt: 7 × 5/6 — slide to estimate the product in wholes.
widget.lowFeedback: Too low — each of the seven groups is nearly a whole one.
widget.highFeedback: Too high — seven groups of just under one cannot pass seven.
widget.successFeedback: About 6 — the exact value is 35/6, which is 5 5/6, just under seven.

predict.reveal: 35 counts sixth-PIECES, not wholes; thirty-five sixths is only about six wholes.

cml.actionGoal: Collect equal groups of a fraction and watch only the COUNT of pieces change for g4x estimate.
invariants: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number collects groups of identical pieces: the denominator names the piece size and holds still, while the numerator counts every piece gathered, which is what keeps g4x estimate a counting problem.
misconceptions: Scaling the denominator along with the numerator, adding the whole number to the numerator, or assuming a product cannot pass one whole.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the denominator DID change when you collected groups, what would happen to the size of each piece?

widget.prompt: Roughly how big is 7 × 5/6, without computing exactly?

options.label: A little less than 7, since 5/6 is nearly a whole
options.feedback: Correct — each group is just under one, so seven of them land just under seven.

options.label: About 35, since 7 × 5 = 35
options.feedback: That ignores the sixths entirely; 35 counts pieces, and 35 sixths is under six wholes.

options.label: Less than one, since 5/6 is a fraction
options.feedback: Taking seven groups of nearly-a-whole cannot land under one whole.

options.label: Exactly 7, since 5/6 rounds to 1
options.feedback: Rounding 5/6 up to 1 gives an estimate of 7, but the true product is slightly BELOW it.
